items.text:
@MIPAGUY The cloud still needs a power supply. I agree with Musk that scaling AI requires power generation and chip production alongside software.

His bet that 1% more electricity use will produce roughly 1% more GDP is a forecast, not an economic law.

Kardashev’s 1964 scale classified civilizations by the energy they could harness, extending to stars and galaxies. Today’s AI buildout makes that connection between energy and capability increasingly tangible.

Musk’s efficiency argument matters just as much: better chips and algorithms can deliver more useful intelligence per watt. Progress means expanding the energy supply while improving what we accomplish with it.

That is why SpaceX’s solar-powered orbital computing plans interest me. Put the computers where sunlight is abundant, then send the results home. Launch economics, heat rejection and reliability still have to work.

A civilization advances both by harnessing more energy and by learning to do more with it.

items.text: @pvncher @weswinder Key design directions:  • One canonical repository/project state rather than unnecessary full clones. • Git worktrees, copy-on-write snapshots, content-addressed storage, and shared Git objects for cheap isolated modifications. • Persistent incremental repository/code indexing rather than every agent rescanning the project. • Shared AST/symbol/dependency/test/build maps. • A durable evidence ledger containing hypotheses, experiments, failures, successful approaches, decisions, and provenance. • Task-specific context packets instead of repeatedly injecting huge project histories. • Context deduplication and provider prompt caching. • Multi-model routing: cheap models for routine work; expensive reasoning only where justified. • A provider-independent worker interface supporting frontier APIs and local/open models. • A commander that decomposes jobs, detects overlapping work, merges discoveries, and terminates unproductive branches. • Structured worker-to-worker handoffs rather than transferring whole conversations. • Independent replay/verifier workers so an agent cannot certify its own claimed success. • Build/test/lint/proof/security gates. • Exact provenance for every file change, command, model call, result, and resource consumed. • Warm dependency/build caches shared safely across execution environments. • Local-first and BYO-compute/BYO-model options. • Complete resource accounting: tokens, cached tokens, inference cost, compute/container time, storage, networking, builds, and external tools. • Cost prediction before launch plus live burn rate and projected completion cost. • Hard budgets at worker, task, project, and organization level. • Automatic detection of loops, repeated searches, repeated file reads, repeated failed patches, and rediscovery of already-known facts. • Negative knowledge: failed approaches should prevent other workers from unknowingly repeating them. • Parallelism only where expected information gain justifies duplication cost. • Persistent project/organization memory surviving individual sessions. • A control-room UI where a user can inspect, stop, redirect, cap, fork, or ask why any worker is consuming resources. • Optimize for VERIFIED USEFUL WORK PER DOLLAR/TOKEN/COMPUTE-MINUTE—not number of agents or time spent running.  The thesis is simple:  DON'T PAY AI TO THINK IN CIRCLES.  Sandboxes should be isolated hands, not isolated brains.

items.text:
AI-enhanced petitions on https://t.co/MMBoNKMyWP: More text, less success | Cornell University

The change was obvious—but in the end, things stayed about the same. Cornell researchers took advantage of online petition website https://t.co/MMBoNKMyWP's gradual rollout of an artificial intelligence writing tool to gauge AI-enhanced language's impact on petition outcomes.

The effect on outcomes? Negligible, at best.

An analysis of 1.5 million petitions showed that the AI writing assistance altered the wording of petitions, increasing their homogeneity and length, but did not improve petition outcomes, according to a research team that included Mor Naaman, the Don and Mibs Follett Professor of Information Science at Cornell Tech, the Jacobs Technion-Cornell Institute at Cornell Tech and the Cornell Ann S. Bowers College of Computing and Information Science.

"That was a surprise for us," said Isabel Corpus, a doctoral student in information science and lead author of "Introducing AI to an Online Petition Platform Changed Outputs but Not Outcomes," which was published Sept. 30 in Nature Human Behaviour.

"There is this existing research that shows AI-generated text is persuasive, it's believable and it can be creative, sometimes more so than people writing alone," Corpus said. "And then on top of that, we would expect that a platform would integrate a tool that would improve outcomes, so we were surprised that it didn't."

In addition to Corpus and Naaman, co-authors included Allison Koenecke, assistant professor of information science at Cornell Tech and Cornell Bowers; and Eric Gilbert, professor in the School of Information at the University of Michigan.

A staggered rollout enabled comparisons

Naaman said he heard about https://t.co/MMBoNKMyWP's introduction of an AI writing assistant a few years ago from an employee of the site. When they looked into it, Corpus discovered that the tool was being rolled out gradually in English-speaking countries—first in the U.S., Great Britain and Canada, and 11 weeks later in Australia. That staggered rollout allowed the team to measure AI's impact by comparing petitions written before and after the introduction of the tool across the different countries.

The researchers hypothesized that, since all four countries followed similar trends in petition style and outcomes before the AI tool's release, differences in trends during and after the 11-week rollout period—Oct. 2 through Dec. 15, 2023—could be attributed to the AI tool.

Although he couldn't say for sure, Naaman suspects the AI writing assistant https://t.co/MMBoNKMyWP employed was trained, in part, on successful petitions the site hosted previously. "We saw in the data that those [AI-enhanced] petitions had the markers of what was successful in the past," he said, noting that https://t.co/MMBoNKMyWP was one of the first online platforms to directly employ an AI writing assistant.

Longer petitions, no improvement in engagement

The team measured the effect of AI on lexical style using three main features: lexical diversity, by calculating the ratio of unique words to total words; readability, determined by measuring the number of words per sentence and syllables per word; and petition length, including text and title.

What stood out was the consistent effect on lexical features: Petitions written with AI's help were longer, with more complicated and varied words.

"We also saw a lot of homogeneity in the language of the titles," Corpus said. "Petitions started calling for people to 'implement,' 'mandate' or 'urge,' whereas before we rarely saw that these words were used."

Using two metrics to gauge petition effectiveness (the share of petitions that reach one comment in 30 days and the share that reach 10 signatures at the time of data collection), the researchers found that outcomes did not improve compared with pre-AI levels and in some cases worsened. The share of petitions that reached one comment after 30 days following the AI tool's introduction in fact decreased by around 5% relative to the pre-AI baseline.

Specificity and sharing may drive support

Naaman said the team had a few theories as to why AI-assisted petitions didn't fare any better than exclusively human-written ones. For one thing, people are suspicious when they feel something is written by a "robot," although he admitted this was very early in the era of AI writing helpers such as ChatGPT. "People didn't have their AI radars as high in 2023," he said.

More likely, he said, AI-generated petitions tended to be less specific and detailed, and the petitioners likely were less committed to sharing their plea more broadly if it was, at least in part, written for them.

"From our research, it seems that people don't sign a petition because they're browsing on https://t.co/MMBoNKMyWP," Corpus said. "They sign a petition or engage with a cause because someone they trust, or an organization they trust, shares it with them. So if there's a decline in shares, then we would expect there to also be like a decline in engagement."

items.text:
Tesla stock rallied on delivery news. Can upcoming earnings justify the AI hype?👇
⠀
Tesla ($TSLA) posted its Q3 2026 production, deliveries, and deployments on October 2, 2026.
⠀
The official table showed total production of 464,391 vehicles, total deliveries of 486,532 vehicles, and energy storage product deployments of 13.7 GWh.
⠀
Deliveries came in about 22,000 vehicles above production.
⠀
Tesla's 8-K filing with the SEC under Item 2.02 confirmed the company released a press release the same day as Exhibit 99.1.
⠀
Tesla said in the official press release that deliveries and energy storage deployments are just two measures of financial performance and shouldn't be viewed as indicators of quarterly financial results.
⠀
Those results depend on multiple factors, including average selling prices, cost of sales, and foreign exchange moves, and Tesla will disclose them in the 10-Q for the quarter ended September 30, 2026.
⠀
-----
⠀
🔴 Follow me on X: @rich_compass
⠀
U.S. stock, crypto, and technical analysis
⠀
-----

▋ Deliveries hit a new 2026 high but dropped 2% from last year
⠀
According to FactSet data, Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles in Q3, about 5.5% above the 461,000 analysts expected.
⠀
This was the second straight quarter above market expectations and Tesla's best single-quarter sales so far this year.
⠀
Against the company-compiled consensus of 461,974, total deliveries were also about 25,000 higher.
⠀
Gary Black of The Future Fund said the result beat his estimate of 470,000 and the market's estimate of about 462,000.
⠀
But compared with 497,099 a year earlier, deliveries were still down about 2%.
⠀
The Q3 2025 number was high partly because some consumers pulled purchases forward before the federal EV tax credit expired.

▋ Model 3 and Y dipped slightly while other models delivered 8295 vehicles
⠀
The official Q3 table showed Tesla's main models, Model 3 and Model Y, delivered 478,237 vehicles, below 481,166 in the same period of 2025.
⠀
Another 8,295 vehicles were "other models" deliveries, mainly the Cybertruck electric pickup, and they may include a small number of other deliveries.
⠀
Tesla stopped production of Model S and Model X earlier this year.

▋ Energy storage missed expectations as analysts point to tight supply
⠀
On energy storage, Tesla deployed 13.7 GWh of products in Q3, below the 15.9 GWh analysts expected.
⠀
After a slow start to the year, analysts had expected Tesla's energy business to heat up in the second half of 2026.
⠀
Analysts also said Tesla's Megapack is critical to meeting power demand driven by US data center buildout.
⠀
William Blair analyst Jed Dorsheimer said in a client report that the growth pace of Tesla's energy storage business has slowed.
⠀
But he said his view on the demand environment was unchanged and attributed the slowdown to supply constraints.

▋ Tesla stock rose over 4% while Rivian Ford and GM dropped
⠀
Yahoo Finance data showed Tesla closed at $370.59 on October 2, 2026, up 4.65% (+$16.48) from the previous close of $354.11.
⠀
On Friday Tesla stock rose 4.7%, while other automakers generally fell that day: Rivian ($RIVN) dropped 3.1%, Ford ($F) dropped 1.4%, and GM ($GM) dropped 1.3%.
⠀
Rival Rivian delivered 19,248 vehicles in Q3, up about 46% from a year earlier, beat market expectations by a bigger margin, and reiterated its July-raised full-year 2026 delivery guidance of 65,000 to 70,000 vehicles, yet the stock fell about 3% that day.
⠀
Legacy automakers also faced pressure in US EV sales, as Ford's Q3 EV sales fell about 80% from a year earlier and General Motors said several EV models saw big Q3 sales declines.
⠀
As of early October, Tesla stock was down about 18% since the start of 2026, while Rivian was down 27%.

▋ Analyst credits gas prices for the delivery beat and rejects FSD hype
⠀
Gary Black of The Future Fund attributed Tesla's Q3 delivery beat mainly to higher gasoline prices, not a demand recovery.
⠀
He said upside momentum may support raising full-year 2026 estimates after Tesla earnings, depending on how much the company spends on AI.
⠀
Gary Black estimates Tesla global inventory is about 12 days of sales, below Q2's 15 days, but above 10 days a year earlier.
⠀
He rejected the view that "Full Self-Driving progress drove deliveries" and argued unsupervised self-driving is becoming a basic threshold for the entire industry.
⠀
He added that without advertising, few buyers outside Tesla supporters know how far the system has progressed.

▋ Annual pace stays below two million as analysts debate the slowdown
⠀
Ross Gerber of Gerber Kawasaki said Tesla's annualized delivery run rate is still below 2 million vehicles per year.
⠀
He called it "massively disappointing" relative to expectations set several years ago.
⠀
Gene Munster of Deepwater Asset Management sees Tesla's 2% annual decline as evidence the "EV winter" is thawing.
⠀
Munster noted the market had expected about a 7% decline, and he expects 2027 delivery growth above 15%, while the market expects close to 9%.
⠀
Based on Q3 deliveries reported by both companies (19,248 vs 486,532), Rivian's deliveries were about one twenty-fifth of Tesla's, while Munster roughly estimated about one twenty-fourth.

▋ The AI narrative drives the stock as investors eye SpaceX merger talk
⠀
UBS ($UBS) analyst Joseph Spak told clients that investors' focus is entirely on Tesla's transformation into a physical AI company.
⠀
He said the stock is driven by narrative and sentiment around future AI possibilities, and that delivery data on release day only "create noise".
⠀
Spak said investors are interested in a possible merger between Tesla and SpaceX, which is run by CEO Elon Musk.
⠀
On Stocktwits, an investing community, users were also disappointed that Tesla only slightly beat expectations, and they emphasized the company's high valuation.

▋ Tesla lines up credit lines with zero borrowings and a $5B liquidity rule
⠀
Tesla signed three credit agreements on September 29, 2026.
⠀
They include a $20 billion three-year delayed draw term loan, an $8 billion five-year revolving credit facility, and a $2 billion 364-day revolving credit facility.
⠀
Tesla said that as of September 29, 2026, there were no borrowings outstanding under those credit facilities, and the company currently does not plan to draw on them in 2026.
⠀
Tesla's credit agreements require the company to maintain at least $5 billion in consolidated liquidity.

▋ Deliveries do not equal profit and full earnings drop on October 21
⠀
The sources checked didn't have specific data on the average selling price of Tesla's Q3 delivery mix, gross margin, or changes in its China market share in Q3, and Tesla only said those financial results depend on average selling prices, costs, foreign exchange, and other factors, and that they'll be disclosed in the 10-Q.
⠀
Tesla announced it will report Q3 2026 financial results after the US market close on October 21, 2026.
⠀
It will hold a Q&A webcast that day at 4:30 PM US Central Time (5:30 PM US Eastern Time, 5:30 AM Taiwan Time on October 22) to discuss financial and business results and outlook.
⠀
Tesla gave only three operating data points on October 2: deliveries, production, and energy storage, while the full earnings after the market close on October 21 will reveal the real profit impact from average selling prices, costs, and foreign exchange.

⚠️ The above is a compilation of public information, not guaranteed to be accurate, and not investment advice.
